conversation.content: Let's design a distributed message queue like Kafka or RabbitMQ. It should handle high throughput, provide durability, and support multiple consumers. Where would you start?

I spent six years working on the Linux kernel — storage subsystem and networking stack. So my instinct is to start with the I/O path because that's what determines the throughput ceiling. Before I design anything: what's the target throughput in messages/sec and bytes/sec? What's the message size distribution? And what's the durability guarantee — can we lose the last few milliseconds of data on a crash, or do we need fsync-level guarantees?
Target: 2 million messages per second, average message size 1KB. Durability: messages must survive single-node failure. Ordering within a partition. Sub-10ms publish latency at p99.

2M messages/sec at 1KB = 2GB/sec raw throughput. With replication factor 3, that's 6GB/sec of disk I/O across the cluster. With metadata overhead, call it 8GB/sec. Modern NVMe SSDs do 3-4 GB/sec sequential writes, so we need at least 2-3 drives just for the write path. But here's where kernel knowledge matters: the question isn't 'can the disk handle it' — it's 'can the software path keep up with the disk?' In many message queues, the bottleneck is the user-kernel boundary: too many syscalls, too many memory copies. Let me design the I/O path to minimize those.
Tell me about the storage engine design — how do messages get written to disk?

The storage engine is an append-only log, partitioned into segments. Each partition is a directory on disk. Within a partition, messages are appended to the active segment file. When the segment reaches a configured size (1GB), we close it and start a new one. This is similar to Kafka's approach, but I'd optimize the write path using kernel primitives. For the write path, three approaches with different performance characteristics. Approach 1 — Traditional write(): application serializes messages into a buffer, calls write() to a file descriptor. The kernel copies the data from user space to the page cache, then eventually flushes to disk. Two memory copies (app buffer -> page cache -> disk DMA buffer), one context switch per syscall. At 2M msgs/sec, that's potentially 2M write() calls/sec — way too many context switches. Fix: batch messages into larger writes. Approach 2 — mmap(): memory-map the segment file. Write messages directly to the mapped region. The kernel handles flushing to disk via its writeback mechanism. Advantage: one fewer copy (no user -> kernel copy, the page cache IS user-accessible memory). Disadvantage: msync() for durability is coarser-grained and harder to control than fsync(). Approach 3 — io_uring: the Linux async I/O interface. Submit batches of write operations to a shared ring buffer with the kernel. The kernel processes them asynchronously. Zero context switches per I/O — submissions and completions happen via shared memory. At 2M messages/sec, I'd batch 1000 messages (1MB) into a single io_uring write submission. That's 2000 submissions/sec instead of 2M syscalls/sec. This is my preferred approach.
How does the consumer read path work? How do you serve 2M messages/sec to consumers?

The read path is where zero-copy really shines. Traditional approach: read data from disk to page cache, copy to user space, copy to a socket buffer, DMA to the network card. That's three copies and two context switches per read. Zero-copy approach using sendfile(): the kernel transfers data directly from the page cache to the socket buffer via DMA. No copies through user space at all. One syscall, zero user-space memory copies. This is exactly how Kafka achieves its legendary read throughput. For the consumer, I'd implement it like this: the consumer sends a fetch request with (partition, offset, max_bytes). The broker locates the segment file containing that offset, computes the file position, and calls sendfile(segment_fd, socket_fd, offset, length). The operating system handles the rest. If the data is still in the page cache (recent messages, which is the common case for tailing consumers), there's zero disk I/O — it's a pure memory-to-network DMA transfer. For consumers that are behind — reading old data not in the page cache — the kernel does read-ahead (automatically prefetches sequential pages), so the disk access pattern is still sequential and fast. I'd tune the read-ahead window: echo 256 > /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/read_ahead_kb for a 256KB read-ahead, which matches our segment I/O pattern well.
Impressive low-level knowledge. How do you handle durability — making sure acknowledged writes survive a crash?

Durability has two levels: single-node (survive process crash) and multi-node (survive hardware failure). Single-node durability: after writing to the log, we need the data on persistent storage, not just in the page cache. Options: fsync() after every write — guarantees durability but limits throughput to about 50K-100K ops/sec (fsync latency on NVMe is 20-50 microseconds). Group fsync — batch writes over a configurable window (say 5ms), then fsync once for the batch. At 2M msgs/sec over 5ms, that's 10K messages per fsync. Throughput is great, but we risk losing up to 5ms of data on crash. fdatasync() instead of fsync() — skips metadata updates (file size, mtime), saving about 30% of the sync cost. For our requirement of surviving single-node failure, we rely on replication. The leader writes to its page cache and replicates to followers. A message is acknowledged only after W replicas confirm receipt (with W=2 for ISR of 3). Even if the leader crashes before fsyncing, at least one follower has the data. This is Kafka's approach: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2. The leader can use lazy fsync (every 1 second) because replication provides the durability guarantee, not local disk sync. This gives us both high throughput and durability.
How does replication work? How do you keep replicas in sync?

Replication follows the leader-follower model, similar to Kafka ISR (In-Sync Replicas). For each partition, one broker is the leader and 2 others are followers. Writes go to the leader. Followers pull data from the leader by sending fetch requests with their current offset — identical to how consumers read, and using the same sendfile() zero-copy path. The leader tracks each follower's position. If a follower falls behind by more than a configurable threshold (say 10 seconds or 10,000 messages), it's removed from the ISR set. A write is considered 'committed' when all ISR members have acknowledged it. The high-water mark (HWM) — the offset up to which all ISR members have replicated — advances as followers catch up. Consumers only see messages below the HWM, ensuring they never read uncommitted data. For leader election: when the leader fails, the controller (a Raft-based metadata service, similar to Kafka's KRaft) selects a new leader from the ISR. The new leader's log is authoritative — any messages the old leader had that weren't replicated are lost. This is the design trade-off: we prioritize availability and throughput over zero-data-loss guarantees for unreplicated messages.
How does the network layer work? How do producers send messages to the broker efficiently?

The network layer is the other half of the performance equation. Traditional approach: one thread per connection, blocking I/O. At 10K producer connections, that's 10K threads — context-switching overhead kills performance. Better: the reactor pattern with epoll (Linux) or kqueue (macOS). One acceptor thread handles new connections. A small pool of I/O threads (one per CPU core) handles reads and writes using epoll_wait(). Each I/O thread manages thousands of connections. But even epoll has overhead — each epoll_wait() is a syscall. For the ultimate approach, I'd use io_uring for network I/O too (Linux 5.6+). io_uring can handle both storage and network I/O in the same submission queue. A single io_uring instance processes disk writes AND network reads/writes. The producer protocol: producers batch messages client-side (configurable batch size and linger time), compress the batch (LZ4 — fast compression, good for network transfer), and send it as a single request. The broker receives the compressed batch, writes it to the log in compressed form (no decompression needed!), and replicates the compressed bytes. Consumers decompress on read. This means compression happens once at the producer, not at the broker — the broker is just moving bytes.
How do you handle consumer groups — multiple consumers reading from the same topic?

Consumer groups provide scalable consumption with exactly-once processing semantics. A consumer group consists of N consumers. The topic's partitions are divided among the group members — each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group. With 100 partitions and 10 consumers, each consumer processes 10 partitions. Partition assignment uses a strategy — range-based or round-robin. The assignment is managed by a group coordinator (a designated broker). When a consumer joins or leaves, the coordinator triggers a rebalance — redistributes partitions among remaining consumers. The rebalance protocol: the coordinator sends a 'revoke' to affected consumers, they commit their offsets, then the coordinator sends the new assignment. During rebalance, consumption pauses — this is the main downside of consumer groups. To minimize rebalance impact: use sticky assignment (keep as many existing assignments as possible), and implement cooperative rebalancing where only affected partitions pause, not the entire group. Each consumer tracks its offset per partition. Offsets are committed to a special internal topic (__consumer_offsets) periodically (every 5 seconds) or on consumer shutdown. This is a regular topic with its own replication — durable and fast.
What happens when a broker node crashes? How does the system recover?

Broker failure triggers two recovery paths. For partitions where the dead broker was a follower: nothing visible happens. The ISR shrinks by one for those partitions. New data is still accepted with the reduced ISR (as long as min.insync.replicas is still met). When the broker recovers, its follower replicas catch up from the leader automatically. For partitions where the dead broker was the leader: the controller detects the failure (via missed heartbeats, timeout 10 seconds), and selects a new leader from the ISR. Leader election takes milliseconds — it's just a metadata update in the controller's Raft log. Producers receive a 'not leader' error on their next request and refresh their metadata to find the new leader. Total disruption: about 10-15 seconds for detection plus a few hundred milliseconds for election. When the dead broker comes back, it needs to resync. Its log may have diverged — it might have uncommitted messages past the HWM that the new leader doesn't have. The recovering broker truncates its log to the HWM and re-fetches from the current leader. This is a critical correctness step — without truncation, we'd have inconsistent replicas. The resync uses the same sendfile() path as normal replication, so catching up on gigabytes of data is fast — limited only by network bandwidth.
How do you handle the case where a slow disk on one broker affects the entire cluster?

Slow disks are insidious because the broker stays 'alive' (heartbeats succeed) but can't keep up with writes. This is the 'gray failure' problem — harder to detect than a clean crash. Detection: monitor per-broker produce latency percentiles. If broker B's p99 write latency exceeds 100ms while others are at 5ms, something is wrong. At the kernel level, I'd monitor /proc/diskstats for the disk's avgqu-sz (average queue depth) and await (average I/O wait time). A healthy NVMe has await under 1ms; a failing drive might show 50ms+. Also monitor dmesg for I/O errors — NVMe drives often log warnings before they fail completely. Mitigation: the ISR mechanism naturally handles this. If a broker with a slow disk falls behind on replication, it drops out of the ISR. If it's a leader and its produce latency exceeds the threshold, the controller can proactively trigger a leader reassignment — 'prefer-leader' election to a faster replica. For the storage layer: RAID is wasteful for message queues (we have application-level replication). Instead, use multiple independent disks with each partition pinned to a specific disk. If one disk fails, only the partitions on that disk are affected. The broker marks those partitions as 'offline' and the controller reassigns their leadership.
How would you handle message ordering across partitions? What if a consumer needs global ordering?

Within a single partition, ordering is guaranteed by construction — the log is append-only with monotonic offsets. Across partitions, there's no global order — that's the fundamental scalability trade-off. If a consumer needs global ordering across all partitions, the options are limited and expensive. Option 1: use a single partition. Throughput limited to one broker's capacity (maybe 500K msgs/sec). Simple but doesn't scale. Option 2: Lamport timestamps. Each producer includes a logical clock in the message. Consumers use the logical clock for ordering. But this only gives causal ordering, not total ordering — concurrent messages from different producers have arbitrary order. Option 3: external sequencer. A lightweight service assigns a global sequence number to every message before it enters the queue. This becomes a bottleneck — a single sequencer can maybe do 1-2M assignments/sec (it's just an atomic increment). For most use cases, I'd push back on the requirement: do you really need global order, or do you need per-key order? Per-key ordering (all messages for a given key go to the same partition) satisfies most real-world requirements and is trivially achieved with key-based partitioning.
We're running short. Any aspects you'd want to highlight or improve?

I want to mention two things I skipped. First, memory management. For a high-throughput message queue, the JVM's garbage collector is the enemy (this is why Kafka's performance is hard to tune). I'd write the broker in Rust or C++ with manual memory management. For the segment files, use pre-allocated file pools to avoid filesystem metadata overhead. For network buffers, use a slab allocator with fixed-size buffers to eliminate memory fragmentation. Second, the metadata and coordination layer. I described it as 'a Raft-based controller' but didn't detail it. This manages partition assignment, broker membership, consumer group coordination, and configuration. It's a critical component that I'd implement as a separate, small cluster — similar to how Kafka moved from ZooKeeper to KRaft. My design was heavily weighted toward the data path performance, which reflects my kernel background. The control plane (API design, admin tooling, monitoring, multi-tenancy) deserves equal attention in a production system.
Your systems programming depth is remarkable — the io_uring, sendfile, page cache, and disk monitoring knowledge is exactly what makes a high-performance message queue work. Excellent interview.

strengths: Extraordinary low-level systems knowledge — io_uring, sendfile, zero-copy, mmap, page cache optimization
Strong durability analysis with nuanced fsync vs replication trade-offs
Excellent gray failure detection using kernel-level disk monitoring metrics
weaknesses: API design was not discussed — no producer/consumer protocol specification
Control plane (admin tools, monitoring dashboards, multi-tenancy) was acknowledged as incomplete
Higher-level features like dead letter queues, message TTL, and priority queues were not mentioned
